sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark.

questions.q: Complete: (a) The empirical formula of fructose is ______ (CH2O / CHO / CHO2). (b) The percentage of oxygen in Fe3O4 is ______ (27.59% / 72.41% / 27.89%) (Fe = 56 u, O = 16 u).
questions.answer:
(a) CH2O – fructose is C6H12O6, simplest ratio C:H:O = 1:2:1.
(b) Molar mass of Fe3O4 = 3 × 56 + 4 × 16 = 232 g.
% O = 64/232 × 100 = 27.59%.

questions.q: State true or false: (a) Molality of a solution changes with temperature. (b) One mole of any substance contains 6.022 × 10^23 particles.
questions.answer: (a) False – molality uses masses, so it does not change. (b) True.

questions.q: Fill in: (a) The law that states that a compound always contains the same elements in the same proportion by mass is the law of ______. (b) 1 amu = ______ kg.
questions.answer: (a) constant proportions (definite proportions). (b) 1.66 × 10^-27 kg.

questions.q: Match: (a) Lavoisier (b) Proust (c) Dalton with (i) multiple proportions (ii) conservation of mass (iii) constant proportions.
Find the number of moles: (a) in 36 g of water (b) in 11.2 L of N2 at STP.
questions.answer:
(a) Molar mass of H2O = 18 g, so 36/18 = 2 mol.
(b) 11.2/22.4 = 0.5 mol.

questions.q: Name the SI units of (a) amount of substance (b) thermodynamic temperature.
questions.answer: (a) mole (mol). (b) kelvin (K).

questions.q: Complete: (a) Mass of 1 mole of a substance in grams is its ______ mass. (b) The reactant that is completely consumed first in a reaction is called the ______.
questions.answer: (a) molar. (b) limiting reagent.

questions.q: Write the number of (a) protons and (b) neutrons in 199Hg (atomic number 80).
questions.answer: (a) Protons = 80. (b) Neutrons = 199 − 80 = 119.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Define one mole. How many particles does it contain?
questions.answer: A mole is the amount of a substance that contains as many elementary entities as there are atoms in 12 g of carbon-12. It contains 6.022 × 10^23 particles (Avogadro constant).

questions.q: State the law of multiple proportions with an example.
questions.answer: When two elements combine to form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in a simple whole-number ratio. Example: carbon and oxygen form CO (12 g C : 16 g O) and CO2 (12 g C : 32 g O); the masses of oxygen are in the ratio 1 : 2.

questions.q: What is an atomic mass unit (amu)?
questions.answer: It is exactly 1/12 of the mass of one carbon-12 atom, equal to 1.66 × 10^-27 kg. Atomic masses are expressed relative to it.

questions.q: Calculate the mole fraction of water in a solution of 10 g glucose in 90 g of water (glucose 180 g mol^-1).
questions.answer:
Moles of glucose = 10/180 = 0.0556; moles of water = 90/18 = 5.
Mole fraction of water = 5/(5 + 0.0556) = 0.989.

questions.q: Calculate the number of moles of carbon dioxide formed when 1 mole of carbon is burnt in excess oxygen. State the law used.
questions.answer: C + O2 → CO2: 1 mol of C gives 1 mol of CO2 (44 g). The mole ratio is given by the balanced equation (conservation of mass).

questions.q: Write any two postulates of Dalton's atomic theory.
questions.answer: 1. Matter consists of indivisible atoms. 2. Atoms of the same element are identical in mass and properties while atoms of different elements differ. (Also: atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios; atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a reaction.)

questions.q: Why is molality preferred over molarity when temperature changes?
questions.answer: Molality is based on the mass of the solvent which does not depend on temperature, whereas molarity depends on the volume of the solution, which expands or contracts with temperature.

questions.q: How many grams of oxygen are needed to burn completely 4 g of hydrogen to form water? (H = 1, O = 16)
questions.answer: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O. 4 g H2 = 2 mol H2 needs 1 mol O2 = 32 g oxygen.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: A compound contains 40% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen. Find its empirical formula. (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
questions.answer:
Moles: C = 40/12 = 3.33; H = 6.7/1 = 6.7; O = 53.3/16 = 3.33.
Dividing by 3.33: C : H : O = 1 : 2 : 1.
Empirical formula = CH2O.

questions.q: What is meant by limiting reagent? 10 g of hydrogen is made to react with 64 g of oxygen. Find which is the limiting reagent. (H = 1, O = 16)
questions.answer:
The limiting reagent is the reactant that is completely used up and decides the amount of product.
2H2 + O2 → 2H2O. Moles of H2 = 10/2 = 5; moles of O2 = 64/32 = 2.
2 mol O2 needs 4 mol H2 only, so oxygen is completely used and is the limiting reagent.

questions.q: State and explain the law of conservation of mass with an example.
questions.answer: In a chemical reaction the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products (Lavoisier). Example: 2 g of hydrogen (2H2 + O2 → 2H2O needs 16 g of oxygen) combine with 16 g of oxygen to give 18 g of water; mass before = 18 g = mass after.

questions.q: Calculate the molarity of a solution containing 4 g of NaOH dissolved in 500 mL of solution (Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1).
questions.answer:
Molar mass of NaOH = 40 g; moles = 4/40 = 0.1 mol.
Volume = 0.5 L.
Molarity = 0.1/0.5 = 0.2 mol L^-1.

questions.q: The molecular mass of a compound is 180 and its empirical formula is CH2O. Find its molecular formula.
questions.answer:
Empirical formula mass = 12 + 2 + 16 = 30.
n = 180/30 = 6.
Molecular formula = (CH2O)6 = C6H12O6.

questions.q: Differentiate between molarity, molality and mole fraction.
questions.answer: Molarity = moles of solute per litre of solution (changes with temperature). Molality = moles of solute per kg of solvent (independent of temperature). Mole fraction = moles of a component divided by total moles (no unit, independent of temperature).

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: (a) State Dalton's atomic theory. (b) Name two laws of chemical combination and state them.
questions.answer:
(a) Matter is made of indivisible atoms; atoms of an element are identical in mass and properties and differ from those of other elements; atoms combine in small whole-number ratios to form compounds; atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a reaction.
(b) Law of conservation of mass: the total mass of reactants equals that of products. Law of constant proportions: a compound always contains the same elements combined in the same mass ratio.

questions.q: Explain the steps of finding the empirical and molecular formula. A compound has 85.7% C and 14.3% H and molar mass 56. Find its molecular formula.
questions.answer:
Steps: percentage → moles (divide by atomic mass) → divide by the smallest → simple whole numbers; molecular formula = n × empirical formula, n = molar mass / empirical mass.
C = 85.7/12 = 7.14; H = 14.3/1 = 14.3; ratio C:H = 1:2, so CH2 (mass 14).
n = 56/14 = 4. Molecular formula C4H8.

questions.q: Define mole and molar mass. Calculate (a) the number of molecules in 4.4 g of CO2 and (b) the volume of 1.6 g of oxygen at STP. (C = 12, O = 16)
questions.answer:
A mole contains 6.022 × 10^23 particles; molar mass is the mass of one mole in grams.
(a) Moles = 4.4/44 = 0.1; molecules = 0.1 × 6.022 × 10^23 = 6.022 × 10^22.
(b) Moles of O2 = 1.6/32 = 0.05; volume = 0.05 × 22.4 = 1.12 L at STP.

questions.q: Explain the concentration terms molarity, molality and mole fraction. Calculate the molality of a solution having 18 g glucose (180 g mol^-1) in 200 g of water.
questions.answer:
Molarity: moles per litre of solution; molality: moles per kg of solvent; mole fraction: moles of component / total moles.
Moles of glucose = 18/180 = 0.1; mass of solvent = 0.2 kg.
Molality = 0.1/0.2 = 0.5 mol kg^-1.
